label: FS AP-N506H Wi-Fi 6 wall-plate access point
description: FS AP-N506H - Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) wall-plate access point for hotel rooms, dormitories and MDUs: dual radio 2x2 MU-MIMO up to 3 Gbps, 300 clients (50 concurrent), 32 SSIDs, 1x 10/100/1000Base-T uplink plus 4x 10/100/1000Base-T RJ45 downlink ports, 802.3af/at PoE or 12V/2A DC, IP41, wall-plate mount.
notes:
Ports and power come from the **comparison table on the FS product pages**, which is the only place these APs publish a port census at all: the product page itself renders marketing copy for a keyless fetch, and the datasheet URLs 404. The table's **column order follows the page you are on** - the page's own product is column 1 and the rest keep catalogue order (N716, N516, N506, N506H, T566D) - which is worth knowing before reading a row across. **The only member with downlink ports:** '1x 10/100/1000Base-T Ethernet Port, 4x 10/100/1000Base-T RJ45, 1x Pass-through Port from Rear to Bottom'. So one uplink, four switched ports and a **pass-through that is not a port at all** - it is a physical coupler carrying a cable from the rear face to the bottom face, so it is deliberately absent from `interfaces`: a lab could cable it and conclude the AP switches traffic it never touches. Power: 'IEEE 802.3 af/at PoE, DC 12V/2A'. 300 max clients, 50 concurrent, 32 SSIDs, IP41, 160.5 x 89.5 x 34 mm - the dimensions and the 'Hotel rooms, apartments, dormitories, MDUs' recommendation are why this is the wall-plate unit.

The AP power inlet carries no wattage: the vendor publishes the PoE **class** and a DC input rating ('DC 12V/2A' is the adapter's rating, not a draw), so no `poeIn` figure is invented. `poeIn: 0` on the other sockets keeps the engine from treating a downlink port as a power inlet.
